moments.title: A loan and its repayments
moments.text: A borrower receives principal and repays the lender over time, usually with interest.

moments.title: Amortization
moments.text: The video calls the process of paying down the loan through regular payments amortization.

moments.title: Payment, interest and principal
moments.text: A bar chart breaks a fixed regular payment into its interest component and the amount that reduces principal.

moments.title: Why interest is initially high
moments.text: Interest is calculated on the outstanding balance. A relatively large balance produces a larger interest charge at the same periodic rate.

moments.title: How the payment mix changes
moments.text: If equal payments reduce the balance, each interest charge falls and more of a fixed payment goes toward reducing principal.

moments.title: Solve a loan with the finance solver
moments.text: The presenter moves from the general explanation to a personal-loan example.

moments.title: Loan terms
moments.text: The example borrows 5000 dollars at a nominal annual rate of 8%, compounded monthly, to be repaid over two years with monthly payments.

moments.title: The calculator shown
moments.text: The video opens the finance solver on a TI-Nspire. The Casio fx-CG50 uses different menus.

moments.title: Enter the known values
moments.text: The setup uses 24 payment periods, 8% annual interest, a present value of 5000, a final loan balance of zero, and 12 payments and compounding periods per year.

moments.title: Payment timing
moments.text: The video assumes end-of-month repayments for the example.

moments.title: Read the payment
moments.text: The solver gives a negative monthly payment of approximately 226 dollars, indicating money leaving the borrower's account under the chosen sign convention.

moments.title: Estimate total repaid
moments.text: The presenter multiplies the rounded payment by 24 and compares the total with the amount borrowed. Rounding each payment affects this estimate.

notes.title: Rounded payment and total interest
notes.text: The video rounds the monthly payment to 226 dollars before estimating the total repaid. That is a useful approximation but changes the interest estimate.
notes.write: Before payment rounding, the mathematical payment is approximately 226.136 dollars and the corresponding total interest is approximately 427.27 dollars. Actual schedules depend on the lender's rounding and final-payment rules.

notes.title: Calculator in the video
notes.text: The demonstration uses a TI-Nspire, so the menu path differs from the Casio fx-CG50.
notes.write: Use the same financial inputs and check the cash-flow signs, frequencies and end-of-period setting on the fx-CG50.

moments.title: The retirement annuity example
moments.text: The video introduces an annuity as an arrangement that provides regular payments after an initial investment.

moments.title: Payments and the provider
moments.text: The presenter discusses the payment stream and gives an illustrative explanation of the provider's return.

moments.title: Fixed annual payments
moments.text: A diagram illustrates an initial annuity and fixed annual withdrawals; the account balance changes over time.

moments.title: A numerical annuity question
moments.text: The presenter moves to a finance-solver example with an initial investment and equal annual withdrawals.

moments.title: Identify the annuity terms
moments.text: The example starts with 500000 dollars, a 6% annual rate and 30 annual payments.

moments.title: The calculator shown
moments.text: The example opens the finance solver on a TI-Nspire and enters the annuity information.

moments.title: Enter periods, rate and present value
moments.text: Use 30 annual payment periods and a 6% annual rate. From the investor's cash-flow perspective, the initial investment is negative.

moments.title: Set the remaining values
moments.text: The video sets the future balance to zero and the annual payment and compounding frequencies to one.

moments.title: Beginning-of-year payments
moments.text: For its example, the video assumes payments at the beginning of each year. This is important when comparing its result with an end-of-year problem.

moments.title: Read the annual withdrawal
moments.text: With beginning-of-year payments, the solver gives approximately 34268 dollars per year.

moments.title: Other possible unknowns
moments.text: Similar questions can ask for a required initial value or interest rate instead of the periodic payment.

notes.title: Payment timing differs from IB exam convention
notes.text: The video assumes payments at the beginning of each year in its example. The syllabus guidance says exam questions use end-of-period payments.
notes.write: Use the timing stated in the question. For the video's figures, beginning-of-year payments are about 34268.35 dollars; end-of-year payments are about 36324.46 dollars.

notes.title: Calculator in the video
notes.text: The demonstration uses a TI-Nspire, not the Casio fx-CG50.
notes.write: Transfer the financial inputs and sign convention to your calculator; check its payment timing before solving.

moments.title: What a finance solver does
moments.text: A time-value-of-money solver relates present value, future value, payments, interest and timing.

moments.title: Opening the solver
moments.text: The video demonstrates the TI-Nspire menu. The Casio fx-CG50 uses different menus.

moments.title: Number of periods
moments.text: $N$ counts payment periods in the setup shown. For monthly payments over two years, $N=24$.

moments.title: Annual interest rate
moments.text: The presenter enters the stated nominal annual rate as a percentage in the calculator field.

moments.title: Present value
moments.text: Present value is the amount at the start of the financial arrangement.

moments.title: Cash-flow signs
moments.text: The video uses a consistent point of view: cash received is positive and cash paid out is negative.

moments.title: Payment per period
moments.text: The payment field is the amount per payment period, with its sign indicating direction of cash flow.

moments.title: Future value
moments.text: Future value is the amount at the end. A fully repaid loan has a remaining balance of zero.

moments.title: Payments per year
moments.text: Monthly, quarterly and annual payments correspond to 12, 4 and 1 payment periods per year.

moments.title: Compounding periods per year
moments.text: Compounding frequency may differ from payment frequency. Enter each field from the terms of the question.

moments.title: Beginning or end of period
moments.text: Choose whether each payment occurs at the beginning or end of its payment period; timing affects the result.

notes.title: Calculator shown in the video
notes.text: The video demonstrates a TI-Nspire. Field names and menus can differ on the Casio fx-CG50.
notes.write: Keep the same cash-flow sign convention and check the payment and compounding frequencies on your calculator.

ican.text: I can distinguish loan principal, interest, repayment and outstanding balance.
I can set up and solve a loan or annuity using a finance solver, with consistent cash-flow signs.
I can distinguish the nominal annual interest rate, payment frequency and compounding frequency.
I can interpret the effect of end-of-period versus beginning-of-period payments.
I can calculate total repayments or withdrawals and explain how rounding and final-payment rules affect the result.
I can check a finance-solver answer using a balance recurrence or a reasonableness check.

ku.text: A repayment on a reducing-balance loan covers interest charged on the outstanding balance; the rest reduces the principal. For fixed payments at a fixed periodic rate, a falling balance reduces the interest component over time.
If the payment $P$ is made at the end of each period and the rate is $i$ per period, the loan balance follows $B_{n+1}=B_n(1+i)-P$. If a payment does not cover interest, the balance can increase.

An annuity consists of a regular stream of payments. In a withdrawal annuity, investment growth and withdrawals together determine the balance; do not assume every annuity must finish at zero unless the question says so.

In a finance solver, $N$ is the number of payment periods, $PV$ the starting value, $PMT$ the payment per period and $FV$ the value at the end. Enter the stated nominal annual rate and set both payments per year and compounding periods per year.

Set the sign convention from one person's viewpoint. For a borrower, money received may be positive and repayments negative; for an investor, the initial investment may be negative and withdrawals positive. Reversing all signs consistently is also valid.

Payment timing matters: beginning-of-period payments have more time to earn interest than end-of-period payments. The syllabus guidance states that exam questions use end-of-period payments; follow the question's explicit timing in other contexts.

Keep unrounded calculator values through intermediate steps. When actual payments are rounded to cents, the final payment may need adjustment. State whether a total uses a rounded payment or the unrounded model.

misc.weak: A 3-year loan with monthly payments has $N=3$.
misc.better: The solver's number of monthly payment periods is $N=3\times12=36$.

misc.weak: Payments per year and compounding periods per year are always equal.
misc.better: Read each frequency from the question. They can be different and need separate inputs.

misc.weak: Enter both a loan received and payments made as positive cash flows.
misc.better: Use opposite signs for money entering and leaving the same person's account.

misc.weak: For an end-of-month payment, subtract the payment before adding that month's interest.
misc.better: In the basic end-of-period model, apply interest to the opening balance, then subtract the payment.

misc.weak: The video's annuity result can be used unchanged if the payments switch from the start to the end of each year.
misc.better: The payment timing changes the value; reset the solver and recalculate.

misc.weak: Multiply a payment rounded to the nearest dollar by the number of periods to obtain the exact total interest.
misc.better: That gives an estimate. Use unrounded values for the mathematical model, and follow any specified payment-rounding and final-payment rules.

terms.text: Identify the number of payment periods, nominal annual rate, principal, final balance, frequencies and payment timing; use a consistent sign convention.
Specify the point in time and whether it is before or after that period's payment.
For a fully repaid loan with the stated payment schedule, subtract the amount borrowed from the total paid. Account for rounding and any different final payment.

gdc.text: Enter the known values in $n$, I%, PV, PMT, FV, P/Y and C/Y. Use the negative key for money flowing in the opposite direction.
Check the end-of-period payment setting and the payment and compounding frequencies before solving. The exact setting sequence should be checked on your calculator.
From the list, select the unknown using [F1] $n$, [F2] I%, [F3] PV, [F4] PMT or [F5] FV. [F1] REPEAT returns to the list.

worked.prompt: A borrower receives a loan of 12000 dollars at a nominal annual interest rate of 6%, compounded monthly. The loan is to be repaid by equal end-of-month payments over 3 years. Assume no fees.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: State the solver inputs for the number of payments, annual rate, present value, future balance and frequencies.
parts.a: $N=36$, $I\%=6$, $PV=+12000$, $FV=0$, $P/Y=12$ and $C/Y=12$. Select end-of-period payments and solve for $PMT$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Find the monthly payment, correct to the nearest cent.
parts.a: The solver gives $PMT\approx-365.063249$. From the borrower's perspective the payment is 365.06 dollars per month to the nearest cent.

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Using the unrounded payment, find the balance just after the twelfth payment.
parts.a: Use the solver for the remaining 24 payments or apply the monthly balance recurrence. The balance is approximately 8236.87 dollars.

parts.label: (d)
parts.q: Estimate the total interest using the unrounded mathematical payment.
parts.a: $36(365.063249\ldots)-12000=1142.2769\ldots$, or 1142.28 dollars. A schedule using rounded payments may have a different final payment.

kq.q: Why can the interest component decrease while the total payment remains fixed?
kq.model: The interest rate is applied to a smaller outstanding balance each period. If the payment is fixed and the loan is reducing, more of each payment goes toward principal.

kq.q: What happens if a payment is less than the interest charged for a period?
kq.model: The payment does not cover the interest, so in the simple balance recurrence the outstanding balance increases.

kq.q: Why does the same annuity have different payments in beginning and end modes?
kq.model: Payments at the beginning and end occur at different times and accumulate or remain invested for different lengths of time. A change in timing changes their present value.

kq.q: Why might 36 rounded payments fail to leave a balance of exactly zero?
kq.model: The exact mathematical payment may lie between cent values. Rounding each payment changes the balance, so a lender may adjust the final payment.
